video_title: Vik Uppal: Real Estate Special Situations With a Flexible Mandate
transcript: [music] >> Vic, thanks so much for joining me. >> Thanks for having me. >> I'd love you to take me back, all the way back to where your initial interest in real estate came from. >> So, I was uh born and raised in Minnesota. Uh my parents were immigrants uh from India. My dad came to get his master's at the University of Minnesota, and he was a engineer by profession. And on the side, he would buy and build real estate. So, mainly kind of single-family homes and townhouses and things like that. And so, as a kid, I kind of grew up in the real estate business, which I spent a lot of time with my dad, and I'd go to construction sites, I'd go to projects, and just see how things were built, or we'd go collect rent. And so, I learned kind of real estate at a very early age, really kind of on the front lines of how things are actually done from building, managing, leasing, so forth. And I became really interested, I would say, kind of when I was high school, so pretty uh young age. And then when I was 18 years old with my dad, we built our first uh multi-family project, which was a 48-unit apartment building. And um at that point, I'd read a lot of books, I obviously had experienced a lot of things with my dad, but I really had no history, obviously, building anything of, you know, significance. And it was a um it was both the best experience, but also it was probably one of the toughest projects because, you know, almost anything that could possibly go wrong went wrong, from dealing with contractors, construction budgets, you know, kind of things like that. But, it really gave me, I think, just a tremendous experience around like, how do you actually build things really on kind of the front lines on a hands-on basis. And then after that, I continued kind of as a developer while I was in college. Uh we built a 124-unit apartment building. I, you know, bought and sold different pieces of land, as well as developed kind of other commercial property all around uh the Twin Cities area. And then I always had this kind of vision of building something or renovating something in downtown Minneapolis. And we'd identified a historic building that we that was owned by a family. And so it was really kind of mismanaged and kind of under-managed. And so we bought that in 2007 really at the kind of the worst time possible right before the financial crisis. And we worked with a lender that we did on kind of all of our project with. They had you know very good reputation in Minnesota. And so we bought the building in 2008 and we used historic tax credits to renovate the property. And the whole kind of thesis was you know this building which was really well located, but it was really kind of under mismanaged as well as you know it had not been upgraded for almost you kind of 100 years. And so we'd bring a lot of the systems to kind of market and that would really greatly enhance the value of it. And so we were kind of 1 year into the renovation and then one day we wake up and our lender has been closed in 2008 by the FDIC. And so you know nothing you could have underwrote going into the deal, nothing obviously you could have expected at that at that time. But it was really kind of my first experience into distressed investing and just how you know unpredictable it can be and just how many variables and things you know can ultimately change and evolve so quickly. And so that kind of set off almost a 2-year very litigious process where we were working with the FDIC trying to get them to fund and obviously dealing with a failed bank. We had contractors that had done work and we had to ultimately figure out okay, how do you pay them? And at this point in the middle of you got 2008 there was no chance to obviously really be able to you know bring in a new lender. And so you know that took me almost kind of 2 years to really be able to work out and was both I think a really great experience, but it was also just really tough experience of like in you know I was 24 years old and you know really rolling up your sleeves and dealing with lawsuits and the FDIC and so forth. And so that took me a couple of years to you know kind of forget that resolved and then you know I really thought about what I wanted to do long-term and you know do I start kind of back over again as a entrepreneur and start you know building kind of real estate in the Twin Cities area and I decided I was going to move to New York. And at that point I didn't have you know kind of any relationships. I didn't know a single person and so I decided to Um and you know it's funny when you're young you kind of think that you know two years feels like a lifetime and so I didn't want to get my MBA cuz I figured I mean I don't want to do something for you know that long of a period of time. And so I decided to go to a one-year masters in real estate program at Columbia. And um knowing that I didn't have any kind of relationships I was kind of like a strange thing cuz I was never a very good student. I was never involved in student body. I decided I was going to run for class president and um I just talked about um you know kind of my experience as an entrepreneur and what I could do kind of as class president and bring that and ultimately I um became the class president. And um I just used viewed it as a really great way to meet people and to build a network and relationships and one day I was sitting in class and a guy named Blake Hutchinson who's now the CEO of OMER's was talking about the value of relationships and he was saying that you know a lot of the things that you you you think about like going into grad school is about the things that you learn but so much of it is about the connections and the things that you make and those really last a lifetime. And you know he was talking about his best friend who he had met while was in the same program at Columbia, a guy named Mark McGoldrick who was um the co-founder of the Special Situations Group at Goldman, this legendary investor and you know really made a big name for himself during the Asian financial crisis and was doing all sorts of really kind of distressed and opportunistic investing. And you know when I was hearing this I said boy this guy sounds like he can walk on water." I mean, it was just like unbelievable like his story and the deals that he was doing. And so, I went to Blake after class and I said, "Could you introduce me to Mark?" And so, he gives me his business card. He said, "Sure, email me." Uh so, I email a couple of times, I don't hear back. And I said, "Look, I got to find a way to meet him." And so, then I went to the Columbia administration. I said, "Did you have any connection to Mark?" And they said, "Look, we we know who he is, but he hasn't We've had no connection with him for almost 20 years." And so, I just kept on kept on kept on. And eventually, Blake had introduced me to Mark. And um at this point, he had left Goldman. He had started a firm called Mount Kellett, which was effectively a spin-off of Goldman Sachs sets. You know, he had raised almost $3 billion the week after Lehman failed. And you think about how difficult fundraising is in any environment, but to do it obviously in that period. And then, he followed that up by raising another, you know, almost $4 billion a few years later. And so, um I met Mark. It was supposed to be kind of a 30-minute coffee. And um I met him in a room very similar to this. And you know, it was just a you know, it was supposed to be kind of a coffee chat. What started off as you know, kind of a take kind of a little bit of an awkward introduction cuz he was not the you know, the most kind of warm and welcoming person. I told him about my life and kind of all these you know, kind of experiences that I had as an entrepreneur and how I kind of started at a very young age. And obviously, that business you know, kind of didn't go as planned. And you know, kind of blew up during the financial crisis. And um and then, we talked a lot about kind of our philosophy on life and investing. And you know, keep in mind at that point, I had no experience kind of in any sort of you know, institutional business. I you know, knew how to use Excel, but like very very high-level. And it ended up being a 4-hour meeting where we just talked so much about philosophy and life. And at the end of it, he said, "Look, why don't you come, you know, work for me as a you know, part-time intern?" Um and so, that kind of started off my um um, know, kind of my journey to uh, you know, where I am today. >> What aspects of that meeting you talk about philosophy of life and things you were thinking about your journey resonated that bubbled up from half hour with a guy who's really busy to a 4-hour conversation? >> I think a lot of it was just around and it's sometimes like when you're an outsider into something, you look at it, you know, how it could be versus how it is. And I think a lot of times when people are in a system, they accept a lot of things of like this is norm and this is exactly how things are done and I looked at an industry where I said, "Look, it doesn't There's so many things that just don't make sense to me." And I had my whole career at up until that point had been thinking like a principal and I saw that with my parents being immigrants and, you know, buying and building kind of, um, real estate and I always looked at it like the alignment that I would see in a lot of these firms like just did not make any sense to me. The focus on, you know, kind of AUM growth did not make any sense to me. Um, and a lot of it was, you know, why was things not done a certain way? And I think because I was an outsider into this industry, you know, I really looked at it for what it could be versus, you know, what it is. And I think, you know, for especially for somebody kind of at that stage of their life, that was something that probably Mark and never heard before and it was less about here's my resume, I went to the best school, I'm an Excel genius, um, versus, you know, just more philosophical and I think that then turned into something that was obviously a huge, um, crossroads in my career that ultimately kind of changed the entire trajectory of my life. >> So, when you stepped in to work with Market McAclett, what did you start to see sitting in an institutional seat for the first time that you hadn't been exposed to as an entrepreneur? >> Yeah, it was interesting because I was working with, you know, some of the best and brightest minds specifically in kind of distressed investing and, you know, at that point McAclett was an $8 billion special sits firm investing in all asset classes throughout the world, had this, you know, incredibly prestigious reputation. And I was starting out as a part-time intern that had no experience in this industry, barely knew how to use Excel. And I remember the first day I showed up and like the HR person was like, "Who are you?" And never saw my resume, right? Literally, it was just like, "Why don't you just start on a Monday?" And that was kind of Mark's philosophy even from like the early days of Goldman of like, you know, if I believe in somebody and it's a true kind of meritocracy, then you have the ability to really rise to the top. And I knew from kind of day one that I was never going to be able to excel by being the strongest in terms of technical skills. And so, you know, you had people that were geniuses in Excel and memos and underwriting. And so, I always thought to myself, like, what can I do to really be able to set myself apart from the crowd? And I thought a lot about like, where's value actually created at investment firms? And how do I actually, even as an intern, like, what can I do to really be able to create value and to be able to separate myself from everyone else. And so, I had look, there was kind of two ways. I have to either be able to find some really unique kind of deals that I think really are something that obviously either Mount Kellett or other firms don't necessarily have access to, or I have to be able to find capital. And so, that was where I really said, you know, for 3 months, I, you know, focused on that. And I ultimately found a couple of really interesting opportunities that we ended up investing in. And that then, you know, led to me joining Mount Kellett full-time, you know, once I graduated from Columbia. >> What happened from there? >> I started there as an intern, and then I part-time intern, and I worked there full-time once I graduated from Columbia. And within 2 years, I went from that to ultimately I was co-head of US real estate investments, which was about 25% of the firm's capital. And it was an incredible experience because, you know, I learned from Mark and some of the best distressed investors in the world and that shaped so much of my thinking around how to invest and how to look for blind spots and you know, really where to kind of find those right type of opportunities in the market and then you know, just overall having an introduction into this entire world. And so I think that was just such incredible experience and you know, especially at a special sits firm like you just see so many unique differentiated things. And that was kind of the whole Mount Kala philosophy of go anywhere, do anything, focus on the best relative value regardless of you know, kind of what form it necessarily comes in and so you know, we were buying companies out of bankruptcy, we were restructuring companies, we were doing development deals, we're doing management buyouts, like so many kind of unique things that just gave me such diversity across, you know, all different types of deals. But I think also again be kind of an outsider like I would look at a lot of things that say like there's just things that don't make sense from a alignment perspective, from a culture perspective like and I would always question like why could something not be done a certain way and that was just always kind of brewing, you know, in my mind and um and I was always focused on like how do you actually outperform and how were firms built in a way that actually allow you to outperform and something that I was always kind of thinking about and then from there I I was a managing director at Fortress in their real estate and their credit funds and same thing learned from some you know, really really amazing people and that you know, shaped so much of my thinking but you know, I really felt like there was a opportunity to create a next generation investment firm really going back to the original principles with a lot of the great firms were built on and so um you know, building a firm that does have the right type of incentives, has the right type of philosophy, has the right type of investment strategy that's flexible and nimble and dynamic and that was really catalyst of starting Maverick. >> So when you went to start Maverick, all of those principles are kind of kind of concepts you hear about, alignment, and the right culture, and being flexible. How did you take what you learned and then put structure around it to be able to put that into action? >> Yeah, look, I think probably any one of your guests or any single any single firm probably says all of these things, right? They say they're flexible and nimble and agile and they have the right type of incentives and the reality is it's just not true. And so, I think that a lot of them either have the right type of intent or they did do those things in the early days of their life cycle, but now as the industry has become much more mature, the focus is a lot more on AUM growth, volume, scale, and these big platforms have effectively become factories where they're, you know, just on they're focused on how do we make as many widgets as we possibly can in every single way. And so, whether that's, you know, on on the investing side, whether that's raising capital and you know, a lot of those organizations have become so big and bureaucratic that there's no way that they possibly could be, you know, flexible and nimble and agile. And so, you know, when I thought about starting a firm, there's really kind of the traditional path of okay, you start something really from scratch and the challenge with that I found was, you know, one, there's a huge amount of business risk and so, you know, having the right type of infrastructure and making sure that you have the right type of processes in place and then also a big part of really being able to outperform over the long run is having a stable capital base. And that's the one thing I looked at a lot of the really great investors who performed well over a long period of time is they have stable capital because so much of things you could even be right over the long term, but over the short term with volatility or things like you could look wrong. And so, you know, having a stable base is so critical. And I think also when I looked at a lot of firms where you're like constantly in this hamster wheel of having to raise and deploy capital, like are you actually focused on investing when and where it makes sense, or are you doing it by necessity? And so, if you're doing it by necessity, again, that creates so much business risk and so much pressure. And so, I went down, you know, a more untraditional path, which I, you know, focused on, you know, could I look at a platform that I felt like was, you know, subscale and was really kind of under-living its potential, but had a really strong base and a really strong foundation. And so, that set off, you know, almost an 18-month process of trying to identify a platform that I felt like I could really utilize as a foundation to build a great firm off of long-term. And so, in February of 2018, I bought a firm called Terra Capital Partners, uh and took over their funds that they managed, which is now uh part of Maverick. >> How did you put all this together? Right, so every time someone wants to start a firm, there's some need for capital. As I said, you know, Mark McGoldrick had the ability from his experience at Goldman to raise $3 and get going. When you went to buy Terra, how did that all come together? >> Yeah, so there was a couple of things. One, which was, you know, the founders of the firm, they were effectively at retirement age. And so, one was in his late 60s, one was in his 70s. And so, you know, it was also at a time when, you know, there was kind of a black cloud around the whole kind of retail investor world. And I think now there's obviously so much interest in, and you see what some of these large platforms really have done. I mean, it's pretty incredible. And I think a lot of it is because the, you know, the TAM is just so massive. And so, they're looking at, "Okay, we've really, you know, we've really kind of tapped out a lot of the institutional investors. And now, you know, here we have this other, you know, very, very large market." And yeah, obviously, like there's a way to really be able to capitalize fully on that. But at that time, you know, there was really few institutional investors that were interested in that, you know, kind of that that that area. And that's again kind of always how my mind has worked, which is, you know, where are there parts of the market where capital is not necessarily flowing rationally, and where do I where can I focus where I can really have more of a unique edge and a differentiation. And so, um that's kind of where it started, and then, you know, this took almost a um almost a 1-year process from when we started talking to ultimately when we um ultimately ended up closing and buying the platform. And then I I capitalized it with a combination of my own personal capital, some family capital, as well as some other institutional relationships that I had that um I've known for a long period of time, very very strong relationships, and that, you know, really helped put me in business. >> What was it that you bought? >> So, I bought the management company um as well as I took over the funds that they managed. >> So, what were Yeah, what were those funds? >> Yeah, so majority of the capital was in a private REIT. Um and so, that was the funds that we took over. That was a uh vehicle that dated back to almost 2009, had a very very strong track record. Um and so, that was the vehicle that I took over, and then also the uh the management company. >> How about the renaming of Maverick? Where'd that come from? >> So, the first 2 years from 2018 to kind of 2020, a lot of the focus was really kind of restructuring the platform in order to be able to set it up to be able to manage more institutional capital. And so, at that period, we didn't raise any outside capital. It was much more focused on, you know, how do we actually improve all of our processes? How do we think about, you know, what's going to be the long-term investment strategy? What do we make sure in terms of the right players in the right seats? And it was actually a really interesting experience of coming into an existing platform that had a certain culture, a certain way of doing things, and then really being able to kind of shift that to looking at things in a very different lens, especially in the long term. And so, that was kind of a 2-year process, and then 2020, COVID hits, and all of a sudden, you know, we're thinking, okay, this is now going to be a really, really great environment, especially more for distress, which based on my experience at Mount Kellett and Fortress, like that to me was going to be you know, kind of a huge opportunity set. So, then starting in kind of end of 2020, we launched our first institutional fund. And then from there, we renamed the platform and the management company Maverick, which you know, was just much more aligned with kind of the philosophy of the philosophy of how I thought about the business, which was you know, having a level of stability, a very, very strong foundation, but also being incredibly agile and nimble. And those the combination of those two things as an investor is so important. So, the name Maverick is derived from a Hindi word called Avik, which means the strength of a diamond, but also the fluidity of water and the flexibility of water. And so, I think those two things are just very emblematic of how the firm is operated, but also the way that you really need to be able to have a unique edge in order to be able to outperform over the long run. >> Once you start raising capital in a traditional institutional structure, how do you maintain the different alignment, the different incentives that you saw the rest of the institutional business gravitate towards over time? >> Look, it's not easy because, you know, anytime you're going against the consensus and especially like market practice, it's very difficult to be able to do. And I think that's why, you know, you see there's this herd mentality of like this is what everyone's doing, that feels safe. But again, like with all my my entire background of like thinking like a principal, I saw like where you would see these firms where you know, very few people were investing in the funds, it was very very few people that were sharing in the carry and the upside. That model never made sense to me, which was you know, how do you not have an environment where everyone is eating their own cooking, where everyone is sharing in the upside and you are shoulder-to-shoulder with all of your partners. Like that to me is a very kind of basic in any business. Like that to me is a very basic level of, you know, what you need to have in order to be able to have the right type of outcomes over the long term. And so, you know, in our in our funds, every single person that is legally eligible by the SEC is invested in the funds. And that's not just the investment team or some of the senior members in the organization. That's across the entire company. And you know, I think what that does is not only provide, you know, a huge level of, you know, the right type of alignment, the right type of skin in the game, but also incentivize the right type of intellectual curiosity. Because people are looking at every single dollar as if it's their own. They're questioning every single thing in a way that does create more complication. And I will have sometimes even now where investors will ask, be like, "Why do you do that? Like does that not create more complication for you?" And the answer to that does. Right? Because of course, like you're having to, you know, answer a lot more questions. And there's a huge educational component to it. But when you're committed to something for the long term, you're willing to put in that hard work in order to be able to get the right outcomes long term. And you know, we think the same thing about the incentive fee, where we share the incentive fee with every single person across the organization. And so, it's a philosophy and a mindset where you're truly thinking like an owner. And again, I think a lot of firms will tell you the exact same thing that we want everyone to think like an owner. But the reality is market practice is not to pay people that way. And market practice is focusing much more on volume and scale. And so, you're incentivizing people to do that. Where our philosophy is much more focused on long-term consistent performance. And we want to make sure that everyone across the organization is incentivized that way. And they're all um they're all steering in the right direction. >> I'd love to start diving into how you do this. The idea of being flexible and nimble is super interesting. It can get difficult when it comes to like how are you filtering through ideas and sourcing ideas. So, how do you go about doing that? >> Well, I think one edge is understanding kind of what If you think about like you said a very basic level, what most firms do, right? So, they they define a investment strategy or their mandate and they say, "We're going to invest in this." Whether it's in commercial real estate or any other kind of asset class and then they go kind of raise capital and they say like, "We're going to you know, we're going to invest in this." And so, it's very kind of targeted and for a lot of institutional investors, then they can you know, figure out okay, well, what bucket do I put you in? You know, are you in credit? Are you in private equity? Are you in real estate? Are you in corporate credit? And so, I know exactly where you fit. And so, that is the traditional model that almost every firm uses, but if you think about that, the problem is like if you have an idea today, in 6 or 12 months like the world is moving so quickly that it's impossible to say where you're going to find the best opportunities. And so, that model like never made sense to me of being beholden to a really rigid investment mandates versus like let's go find the best opportunities, whatever form that ultimately ends up coming in. And so, you know, kind of at Maverick, what we ultimately do is we said, "Look, let's keep a very flexible investment strategy and let's let the opportunity shape where we ultimately invest." Now, our standards of our number one priority is capital preservation. We want to make sure everything we invest in has huge downside protection, margin of safety, uh yet we're generating you know, attractive risk-adjusted returns, but having a very, very flexible mandate. Now, a lot of our larger peers, they do those things, but they typically do it with uh different funds, different teams, and across a big organization, it is very hard to be completely integrated. And so, some of the best opportunities we end up finding are these tweener deals that end up not fitting with this fund or this team and they somehow get lost in the ether and then we find those and figure out like how can we capitalize that. And so, that means we're investing across all different markets, public, private, debt, equity. And so, it's a, you know, really, really big funnel and the addressable market for the stuff that we do is incredibly wide, but that allows us to be very patient, very disciplined, and make sure that we're only focused on and moving forward with the highest conviction opportunities. >> When you're communicating to whoever might be showing you opportunities, whether it's peers or, you know, folks selling assets, how do you let them know what the Maverick deal looks like so that they bring it to you? >> There's a huge educational component because there's no typical deal, there's no typical kind of structure. It's much more around providing, you know, customized solution to that opportunity. And so, I think that's both a blessing and sometimes it can be a huge challenge because you're like, "Okay, you do all of this stuff." Again, from the investor standpoint, where exactly do I put you? And I think that's sometimes is a challenge for us cuz we say, "Well, we don't want to be in a bucket because the challenge with the buckets is that then you're very constrained and doesn't give you the ability to focus on the highest conviction opportunities and it leads to a lot of forced investing and you could see so many examples of that where they, over the last, you know, number of years. Um, and I think from a deal flow perspective, while there's an education component, it's a huge benefit because it allows us to look at a situation and say, "What can we do for this situation versus we have to fit something and we have to impress upon our counterparty because that's what our mandate allows." And so, you know, so many of our deals will look a certain way when we'll start to look at them and by the time we ultimately end up closing, they look completely different. And I think that flexibility does allow us then to figure out, "Okay, how do we structure something in the best way for this deal?" And that again, I think without having those type of restraints, it allows us to build something in a way that ultimately gives us the things that we're looking for. >> As you start to filter what comes in the door, what are the things that draw your eye to go spend more time on? >> Our number one priority in anything that we we look for is capital preservation. And so, the first thing that we're think we're looking at is you know, is there a clear line of sight to how we get our money back? And are we accounting for both the known risk as well as the unknown risk? And you know, if you look at my career, I mean, a lot of it has been defined by a lot of ups and downs. And like for that situation that I mentioned that happened to me during the global financial crisis, like that's not anything that I could have underwrote going into that deal of your lender is going to be closed by the FDIC. And so, a lot of that has shaped my thinking of you have to build in a lot of buffer for the things that you can understand and you can know that they're risk going into any deal. And there's always these things that are completely unpredictable that you have to be able to account for. And so, that's the first kind of thing that we're constantly focused on is how do we make sure that we build in enough downside protection that there's clear line of sight to how we get our money back. I'd say the second thing, and this is a big part of our strategy, is how do we focus in the areas in the market where capital is not necessarily flowing rationally? Because that's what allows you to have a big competitive edge. And so, that could be deals that are going to be too small for a lot of our larger peers, that could be business plans or certain industries that could be out of favor. And especially that, like you have to be comfortable when you're going against the consensus of you know, dealing with a lot of scrutiny both from a investor perspective, but also from a public perspective. And so, I think that you have to be willing to withstand that and obviously have a lot of conviction in the things that you're doing. But that's a big part of what we look for is what how what's our competitive edge? How do we find places in the market where capital is not necessarily flowing? And then, how do we build the right type of structure in those investments that gives us enough downside protection and there's clear line of sight to how we get our money back. >> Is there anything you do out of consensus in your in your underwriting process? >> I would say that we're constantly stress testing, you know, both you know, kind of all of our assumptions. We're looking at again what happens in these kind of draconian situations. I think our process is very fluid and so there's not one specific, okay, we're exactly doing this and it's kind of rinse and repeat and I think for a lot of platforms you're doing more commoditized type of transactions, you have more of a factory model, you can do that. And so a lot of what we do is by maintaining flexibility and figuring out how do we make sure we have the right process, but how do we maintain that right type of flexibility to be able to adapt depending on the situations. And so no two deals, no two situations are going to look the exact same and that's where, you know, making sure we run the platform in a way that's very entrepreneurial is an important important part of what we do. >> How do you organize your team to go after opportunities and think this way? >> I would say it's taken a lot of that effort and so it's not just like a philosophy that, you know, everyone kind of understands right away and I think that's one of the things both in terms of the incentive conversation, but also from an investment strategy perspective of being open to, you know, such a wide funnel and just you're constantly triaging different deals and you're constantly looking for the right type of opportunities all over the place. I think now, uh, being so many years into it our team has really developed both the right from a cultural perspective where there's, you know, a lot of information flow, everyone sits, you know, very close to each other. We don't have multiple offices both with our investment team and asset management team and, you know, I think that's really important because you, you know, you learn from both obviously the investment side, but then you learn from your asset management servicing team on what's actually worked and what, you know, has not worked. Now our investment team everyone is generalists and so they maintain obviously a lot of flexibility how they uh, invest. Of course people have, you know, more sector knowledge or may have certain relationships depending on deals or, you know, so forth, but, you know, it's it's definitely a process and so we're constantly trying to make sure that people keep an open mind and constantly you got to re-questioning where the best places are to invest. I also think with this type of philosophy and you know what we're doing is do you have to be okay sitting on your hands and not doing anything for sometimes longer periods of time.
